passage: Dear Bhua ji, You asked on the phone why I was holding a ladle when you visited, so let me explain properly. Disha and I made a chart for the fridge. Disha works late on Tuesdays and Thursdays, so those nights I cook, and on weekends Disha cooks because she enjoys it. I do the laundry; she handles the bills because she is quicker with numbers. We pay our salaries into one account for the household and keep a little of our own. Every Sunday we sit for twenty minutes and change the chart if anything feels unfair. When you raised your eyebrows, I nearly apologised. Then I saw Disha bring you tea and sit beside you, and I realised you were only surprised. Please give it some time. Come again in March, and I'll make you my dal. Gurpreet

qa.q: On which nights does Gurpreet cook?
qa.a: Gurpreet cooks on Tuesdays and Thursdays, when Disha works late.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel when Bhua raised her eyebrows?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt uneasy and self-conscious and nearly apologised. Then Gurpreet realised that Bhua was only surprised.

qa.q: Which choice by the couple helps keep the arrangement fair over time?
qa.a: They sit together for twenty minutes every Sunday and change the chart if anything feels unfair, so the sharing keeps being talked about.

qa.q: How might Bhua have felt seeing Gurpreet with a ladle?
qa.a: Probably surprised and unsure, since the eyebrows went up. Disha bringing tea and sitting beside her suggests a warm welcome that may help her adjust.

grounding: A young couple divides cooking, care and money by ability and time rather than by gender, talks regularly about fairness and gives an elder gentle patience.

passage: People ask how we manage, my husband Kiran and I. Honestly, we never decided by who's the man or the woman. I work night shifts at a call centre in Bengaluru, so Kiran cooks dinner on those days and I make the big Sunday meal because I enjoy it. Kiran pays the electricity and broadband; I do the grocery list because I can do it during my break. We check in every Saturday over tea and swap things if one of us is tired. At first his mother, Jahnavi Amma, would come from Mysuru and hover in the kitchen saying, "Let me do it, he shouldn't." I didn't argue. I just kept saying, "He likes cooking, Amma, taste it." By her third visit she was handing him the onions. Some things take time, and she's trying. Sangeeta

qa.q: Where does Sangeeta work night shifts?
qa.a: Sangeeta works night shifts at a call centre in Bengaluru.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta feel about Jahnavi Amma's hovering, and what shows it?
qa.a: Sangeeta feels calm and hopeful rather than annoyed. Sangeeta does not argue, keeps saying "taste it", and notes that Amma is trying.

qa.q: Which choice by Sangeeta helped Jahnavi Amma adjust?
qa.a: Sangeeta chose not to argue and simply kept saying that Kiran likes cooking and inviting her to taste it, which gave her time to change.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi Amma see her son cooking?
qa.a: At first as something to fix, out of habit and care, since she said he shouldn't. By her third visit she hands him the onions, which shows she is adjusting.

grounding: A young couple divides cooking, care and money by ability and time rather than gender, checks in regularly, and shows patience as an elder adjusts.

passage:
I stayed with my brother Asif and his wife Dilnaz for a week in their Hyderabad flat, and I kept noticing the whiteboard on the fridge.
It said things like "Mon: D cooks, A dishes" and "Rent: A. Groceries: D. Ammi's medicines: both." On Wednesday Dilnaz had a late shift, so Asif made the biryani, badly, and they laughed about it.
On Friday Ammi came to visit. She saw Asif washing the pressure cooker and said, "Dilnaz, beta, you let him do this?" Dilnaz didn't argue. She said, "He's better at scrubbing, Ammi. I'm better at bills." Ammi frowned, but later I saw her reading the whiteboard.
On Sunday night they sat on the sofa and redid the whole week's list together. It took ten minutes. I don't know if it's always this easy for them, but it looked fair.

qa.q: What did the whiteboard say about Ammi's medicines?
qa.a: It said, "Ammi's medicines: both."

qa.q: What might Ammi have been feeling when she saw Asif washing the pressure cooker?
qa.a: She seemed surprised and a little uncomfortable, perhaps worried that people would judge the new daughter-in-law for letting her son do housework.

qa.q: Why was Dilnaz's answer to Ammi a wise one?
qa.a: Dilnaz stayed gentle and explained the split by ability, not gender, giving Ammi time to adjust instead of starting an argument.

qa.q: Why might Asif and Dilnaz redo the list every Sunday?
qa.a: Their shifts and weeks change, so talking regularly keeps the split fair rather than fixed.

grounding: A sibling observes a young couple dividing cooking, chores and money by ability and time, talking regularly and giving an elder patience to adjust.

passage:
Week one. Jomon's father, Lalit Appachan, came to stay after his surgery. On the first morning he watched Jomon make appam while Jomon's wife, Reshma, left for her early hospital shift. "In my house, a son didn't enter the kitchen," Appachan muttered.
Week two. Reshma and Jomon sat at the table on Sunday night with a notebook. She had nights this month; he worked from home. "You do breakfasts and Appachan's physio. I do dinners and the bills," she said. They wrote it down. Appachan pretended to read the newspaper.
Week four. Jomon woke to find his father at the stove, clumsily stirring rice kanji. "Reshma is tired. I can do this much," Appachan said gruffly. Reshma, back from her shift, stopped in the doorway and smiled at Jomon, and neither of them said a word to spoil it.

qa.q: What did Jomon and Reshma use to plan the work?
qa.a: They sat at the table on Sunday night with a notebook and wrote it down.

qa.q: How might Reshma have felt when she saw Appachan at the stove?
qa.a: She was probably touched and pleased, seeing that the elder who had muttered in week one was now helping.

qa.q: What helped Appachan adjust, and why?
qa.a: Jomon and Reshma didn't argue with him; they quietly shared the work by time and ability and let him watch, giving him patience to change on his own.

qa.q: How does Appachan see the kitchen differently by week four?
qa.a: At first he believed a son should not enter the kitchen, but by week four he sees that Reshma is tired and helps himself.

grounding: Over several weeks, a young couple share cooking, care and money by time and ability, and an elder slowly adjusts with patience.

passage:
Tejas, you asked me why your grandfather made the tea every morning of his life. Sit. I'll tell you.
When we married in 1986, I was a bride of twenty-four and teaching at the girls' college, and he worked shifts at the post office. My mother-in-law expected me to do everything at home as well. For three months I tried. I was so tired I fell asleep marking papers.
One Sunday he found me like that. He said, "Sarita, this isn't fair. Let's divide it by who's home and who's better at what." He was better at tea and markets. I was better at accounts. We made a list, and every Sunday we checked it.
His mother was shocked for a year. We were patient. By the end she was telling the neighbours her son made the best tea on the street.
So, Tejas, when you marry, talk every week.

qa.q: What year did Sarita marry?
qa.a: Sarita married in 1986.

qa.q: How was Sarita feeling in the first three months of marriage?
qa.a: She was exhausted and overwhelmed, so tired she fell asleep marking papers while trying to do all the housework alone.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sarita's story?
qa.a: It came when her husband found her asleep and suggested dividing work by who was home and who was better at what, with a weekly check.

qa.q: How did the mother-in-law's view change over time?
qa.a: She was shocked for a year, but with the couple's patience she came to boast that her son made the best tea on the street.

grounding: An elder recalls how she and her husband divided home work by time and ability, talked weekly, and patiently helped an elder adjust.

passage: Tarun's mother was arriving on the 7:40 train, and at six the pressure cooker's whistle gave out. Neelam, who cooked faster, took over the dal on the small burner while her husband Tarun, who had the car and a free evening, drove to the station. The notebook on their fridge still showed what they had agreed last Sunday: she handled the rent transfer, he handled groceries and his mother's clinic visits, and they would look at it again next week. At dinner his mother watched Tarun clear the plates. "In our house, the boys never touched the kitchen." Neelam felt her jaw tighten. Tarun only smiled. "Amma, Neelam cooks better. I wash better." Later, holding a wet steel tumbler, his mother quietly asked him where the dish soap was kept.

qa.q: What time was Tarun's mother's train arriving?
qa.a: Her train was arriving at 7:40.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when her mother-in-law said the boys never touched the kitchen?
qa.a: Neelam felt irritated and a little defensive; her jaw tightened, though she let Tarun answer.

qa.q: What small habit helps this couple keep their split fair?
qa.a: Writing the agreement in a notebook and looking at it again each week keeps the split open to talk, so skill and time decide rather than old habits.

qa.q: How might Tarun's mother be seeing this way of running a home?
qa.a: It is unfamiliar to her and she voices the old rule, but asking where the dish soap is kept suggests she is slowly starting to adjust.

grounding: It illustrates a young couple sharing cooking, errands and money by skill and time, reviewing it regularly, and giving an elder room to adjust.
